definition: Music of antiquity: Greek, Roman and other ancient traditions, known from fragments and treatises.
not: Modern reconstructions, or later works on ancient subjects

definition: European sacred and secular music before about 1400: chant, troubadours and trouvères, Ars antiqua, Ars nova.
not: Later chant-based or neo-medieval works (tag their own period)

definition: Vocal and instrumental polyphony of the 15th and 16th centuries: Franco-Flemish, Roman and Venetian schools, the madrigal.
not: Later pieces in the old style (stile antico)

definition: Basso continuo, concertato writing and contrapuntal forms of about 1600–1750.
not: 20th-century pastiche of Baroque forms (neoclassicism)

definition: Galant and High Classical style: periodic phrasing, sonata form, mainly homophonic textures.
not: 'Classical music' in the broad sense; 20th-century neoclassicism

definition: Nineteenth-century Romantic language: expanded tonal harmony, lyrical melody, character pieces, programme music. Judged by language: a composer who keeps this idiom into the 20th century stays romantic.
not: Post-Wagnerian fin-de-siècle idiom (late_romantic)

definition: Fin-de-siècle and post-Romantic language: post-Wagnerian chromaticism, very large forms and forces, often carried well into the 20th century. Activity after 1880 alone is not enough.
typical: Mahler, Richard Strauss, Reger, Rachmaninoff, Elgar
not: Earlier 19th-century romantic; impressionism; atonal expressionism
source: Wikidata post-romanticism Q1125039, late romantic music Q136774417; the dump also maps Romantic music Q207591 and Romanticism Q37068 here

definition: Music written mainly in 1900–1945 in a 20th-century idiom that no finer tag fits: extended tonality, modality, new rhythmic idioms.
typical: A fallback: prefer a movement tag when a source names one
not: Post-1945 output (modern); a plainly 19th-century idiom (romantic or late_romantic)

definition: Harmony and timbre used for colour: parallel chords, whole-tone and modal scales, static harmony, evocative titles.
not: Expressionism; late-Romantic chromaticism

definition: Extreme expressive intensity, often atonal or hyper-chromatic, with fragmented forms.
not: Twelve-tone works (serialism); atonality without that intensity (atonal_modernism)

definition: Art music built on a national or folk idiom: folk tunes, dances, modes, national subjects and genres. Folk-song arrangements count here when the composer also writes original works in the idiom.
typical: Smetana, Dvořák, Grieg, Albéniz, Bartók, Kodály
not: Traditional music itself (traditional_folk); a single folk-song arrangement in an otherwise different output
source: Wikidata musical nationalism Q1196170; the dump also maps traditional folk music Q235858, sardana Q1413570 and zarzuela Q148163 here

definition: A 20th-century return to pre-Romantic forms and textures: clarity, motor rhythms, Baroque or Classical models, often with ironic harmony.
typical: Stravinsky (1920–1951), Poulenc, Hindemith, Prokofiev's Classical Symphony
not: Baroque or Classical music itself
source: Wikidata neoclassicism Q535611, neoclassical music Q106576145

definition: Free atonal or modernist pitch language without strict serial technique.
not: Twelve-tone or serial works (serialism); expressionism

definition: Twelve-tone technique, or serial organisation of pitch and other parameters, including post-serial practice.
not: Free atonality (atonal_modernism, expressionism)
source: Wikidata serialism Q507246, twelve-tone technique Q221686

definition: Post-1945 classical music in a 20th-century idiom that no finer tag fits: modal, extended-tonal or freely chromatic contemporary writing.
typical: A fallback: prefer a movement tag when a source names one
not: Output mainly before 1945 (early_20th_century); a plainly 19th-century idiom (romantic or late_romantic)

definition: Experimental and radical practice: indeterminacy, graphic scores, extended techniques, music theatre, happenings, Fluxus.
not: Music that is only dissonant (atonal_modernism)
source: Wikidata avant-garde music Q2332751, experimental music Q1640319, Fluxus Q108908, Q102932

definition: Tape music, musique concrète, live electronics, fixed-media or computer music as a main part of the output. List it first when it is the main output; add avant_garde second only when indeterminacy, graphic scores and the like are also central.
typical: Pierre Schaeffer, Pierre Henry, Daphne Oram
not: One or two works with tape in an otherwise instrumental output
source: Wikidata electroacoustic music Q1326777, musique concrète Q823560

definition: Steady pulse, repetition and gradual process over static or slowly changing, mostly consonant harmony.
not: Simple or tonal music without repetitive process

definition: Builds on minimalism's pulse and repetition with more harmonic motion, melody or formal contrast.
typical: John Adams, Michael Torke, David Lang
not: Classic process minimalism (minimalism)

definition: Harmony and form derived from acoustic spectra: the harmonic series, timbre analysis, slow transformations.
not: Colouristic harmony in general (impressionism)

definition: Deliberate collage or juxtaposition of historical styles and quotations within a work.
not: Writing in one older style (neoclassicism)

definition: Jazz, stride or other jazz-idiom composition as a main part of the output.
typical: Jelly Roll Morton, James P. Johnson, Duke Ellington
not: Ragtime itself (tag its period, mostly early_20th_century); concert works with jazz influence (Ravel, Milhaud: tag their own style)

definition: Traditional or folk repertoire itself: anonymous songs and dances, or a collector's editions of them. Only when the output is mainly such collections or editions.
typical: Folk-song collectors whose output is mainly such collections
not: Art music in a national idiom (national_folk)

definition: A classical tradition outside the Western one: Hindustani, Carnatic, Arabic or Persian art music, East Asian court music.
not: Western art music on non-Western subjects
